Whether or not An Ark is a truly original experiment, its results are dispiritingly bland.
While it’s fascinating to complicate a near-future in which theater can survive without actors physically present, An Ark remains more a proof-of-concept curiosity than a revelation.
Neither Simons’ lyricism nor producer Todd Eckert’s pioneering mixed reality will work for everybody.
Nonetheless, the overall experience proves haunting.
You are open-minded enough to applaud the effort of Eckert and director Sarah Frankcom, but you are not convinced that this is an endeavor worth pursuing.
As beguiling as these actors are – and they are an exquisite ensemble – they are not provided with much of a hook to pull us in and hold us close.

Whether that passage feels like profound communion or a beautifully engineered provocation may depend on how willingly one surrendered—but the seriousness of its invitation, and the quiet weight it leaves behind, are unmistakable.
And like that film’s unique POV cinematography, clever presentation here, skillfully realized by veteran director Roberta Uno, is this show’s biggest asset.
But as for being a piece of theater, An Ark is lost at sea.
Ark feels like an example of tech for its own sake.
